segments.title: Postwar navies diverge from a shared carrier starting point
segments.body: The episode asks what post-World War I navies wanted from naval aviation before aircraft carriers became mature systems. Hermes, Hosho, and Langley all draw on wartime experience, but each navy adapts the idea to its own strategic geography and institutional needs. Hermes is the clearest early divergence because the Royal Navy continues building her after deciding that her air group is too small for a first-line strike carrier. The Washington Naval Treaty adds another layer of compromise by treating different navies as if they could accept the same limits without the same missions.

evidence.note: The transcript says the video compares Hermes, Hosho, and Langley in the immediate postwar environment and what navies envisaged for naval aviation.
The transcript says the ships show national appreciation of naval aviation and mark the starting point of divergent carrier development.
The transcript warns against a single right way to develop naval aviation and notes treaty compromises.
The transcript describes naval aviation as immature and treats these carriers as early searches for knowledge.

segments.summary: The opening frames Hermes, Hosho, and Langley as early carrier answers shaped by national strategy rather than by one universal design path.

segments.title: Furious separates wartime improvisation from postwar carrier learning
segments.body: Furious separates emergency wartime development from the more deliberate carrier experiments that followed. Her evolution moves from spotting and reconnaissance toward strike aircraft and a broader air group under pressure to attack the German fleet at Wilhelmshaven. During the war, urgency rewards a workable capability that can be used immediately rather than a fully matured system. After the Armistice, falling budgets, demobilisation, and the disposal of old ships create new constraints, while navies gain time to reconsider their requirements. The first postwar carriers therefore make more sense as learning platforms shaped by peacetime choices than as smaller versions of later fleet carriers.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Furious to trace wartime movement from spotting and reconnaissance toward strike aviation under pressure for immediate results.
The transcript contrasts postwar funding cuts and demobilisation with the new opportunity to step back and develop naval aviation more deliberately.

segments.summary: Furious shows how wartime pressure accelerated the move from spotting aircraft to strike aviation, while peace gave navies time to reassess what carriers should become.

segments.title: Langley gives the US Navy a small carrier laboratory
segments.body: Langley matters even though she looks tiny beside Lexington and Saratoga. The Washington Naval Treaty protects existing experimental carriers, making her a legal and practical starting point for the United States. Her conversion lets the Navy test technologies and operating ideas before it builds Ranger, its first carrier designed from the keel up. Her torpedo bombers and fighters show the US Navy looking for offensive power while working under tight financial and political limits.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces Langley as CV-1 and the original American carrier.
The transcript explains the Washington Naval Treaty exemption for experimental carriers and says Langley is the American beneficiary.
The transcript says Langley lets the Americans start small and is the starting point for American naval aviation growth.
The transcript ties Langley's air group to strike aircraft, fighters, and the US Navy seeking offensive capability.

segments.summary: USS Langley appears as the US Navy's first carrier step: an experimental conversion that lets the fleet learn before Lexington and Saratoga arrive.

segments.title: Langley's open hangar reflects a Pacific-centered outlook
segments.body: Langley's physical arrangement reflects the US Navy's westward strategic outlook. Although the ship was converted at Norfolk, her open-sided hangar would expose fragile early aircraft to harsher Atlantic conditions. That tradeoff makes more sense within the vast spaces and different operating assumptions of the Pacific. The design shows how geography shaped even an experimental carrier's practical compromises.

evidence.note: The transcript says much American naval-aviation development is focused on operating in the Pacific and frames this as a westward outlook.
The transcript contrasts Langley's Norfolk conversion with her open sides and open hangar, asking what Atlantic conditions would do to early aircraft.

segments.summary: Langley's open-sided hangar helps reveal how strongly early American carrier thinking was oriented toward Pacific operations rather than North Atlantic weather.

segments.title: The Douglas DT highlights source loss and aircraft preservation
segments.body: An aside on Langley's Douglas DT turns from carrier design to the fragility of early aviation evidence. The disputed possibility that Norwegian aircraft attacked German invasion forces in 1940 needs further investigation. Occupation and fear of reprisals could help explain why records of such an attack disappeared, so the episode remains uncertain. The physical record is equally thin: ninety Douglas DTs were built, and none survives. Source loss and the decay of early aircraft make this part of naval-aviation history especially difficult to reconstruct.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses the uncertain claim that Norwegian Douglas DTs attacked German forces and why occupation could have erased records.
The transcript says ninety Douglas DTs were built and none survives.

segments.summary: A Douglas DT aside links a disputed Norwegian wartime attack to the disappearance of records and every surviving example of the aircraft.

segments.title: Lexington and Saratoga expose carrier-gun tradeoffs
segments.body: Langley's strike experiments sit alongside Lexington and Saratoga entering the US Navy's scouting and reconnaissance force. The converted battlecruisers raise questions about the value of mounting 8-inch guns high in an aircraft carrier. The guns and their supporting structure add topweight, and using them would turn a large, fragile aviation asset toward surface combat instead of keeping distance and launching aircraft. Removing that battery could free weight for armour or equipment that supports more aircraft and faster launch-and-recovery cycles. Carrier design has to follow the ship's aviation mission instead of preserving cruiser or battlecruiser habits.

evidence.note: The transcript places Lexington and Saratoga in the scouting and reconnaissance force and considers the value of their battlecruiser lineage.
The transcript questions the topweight and tactical value of 8-inch carrier guns and suggests armour or aircraft support as alternative uses for the weight.

segments.summary: The American battlecruiser conversions prompt a design question: should a carrier carry heavy guns, or devote that weight and maneuvering freedom to aircraft operations?

segments.title: Langley exercises make torpedo air attack a fleet problem
segments.body: Langley's first exercises show an experimental carrier beginning to reshape fleet assumptions. Torpedo-bomber attacks against unescorted battleships are artificial in setup, but the Navy treats the exercise as a worst-case test worth learning from. Arkansas receives eight simulated hits from eighteen torpedoes, while other weapons continue into the formation, exposing how slowly the battle line can evade a concentrated aerial attack. The design consequence is air-group arithmetic: if some aircraft will be lost or blocked, the carrier has to launch enough for the required number to reach the target.

evidence.note: The transcript describes early exercises attacking battleships with fighters and torpedo bombers.
The transcript says the exercise showed battleships could not simply maneuver away from a concentrated torpedo attack.
The transcript says Langley helped drive later exercises and the need to calculate enough aircraft to reach a target.
The transcript says American geography and infrastructure let the US Navy concentrate on carrier air group size.

segments.summary: Early Langley exercises use fighters and torpedo bombers against battleships, pushing the US Navy toward larger carrier air groups.

segments.title: Hosho starts Japan's carrier and aircraft learning curve
segments.body: Hosho is more than a small first carrier. Japan observes British wartime carrier work, changes course from planned seaplane carriers, and builds a full-length flight-deck carrier from scratch. British influence then helps Mitsubishi develop fighters, while Japanese choices aim for a workable development path rather than an instant leap to perfection. Hosho becomes a ship-design experiment, an aviation school, and a foundation for domestic aircraft manufacture.

evidence.note: The transcript says Hosho commissioned in December 1922 after Japan changed from seaplane-carrier plans to wanting an aircraft carrier.
The transcript compares Hosho, Ryujo, and Soryu to show how larger carriers become more aircraft-efficient.
The transcript identifies Hosho's early torpedo bombers and fighters, including British design influence on Mitsubishi.
The transcript compares Sparrowhawk and 1MF performance and says Japan is building infrastructure and knowledge without creating a disaster.
The transcript calls Hosho Japan's first full-length carrier built from scratch.

segments.summary: Hosho shows Japan shifting from seaplane-carrier plans to a true flight-deck carrier while building the aircraft and industrial skills it needs.

segments.title: Hosho reveals carrier scaling and early flight-deck hazards
segments.body: The comparison among Hosho, Ryujo, and Soryu shows that carrier capacity does not scale in a simple one-aircraft-per-ton fashion. Soryu carries nearly five times Hosho's aircraft on a little more than twice the standard displacement, while Ryujo demonstrates the instability risk of forcing a large air group onto a small hull. The discussion then turns to flight-deck safety, where a flush deck gives early pilots fewer visual cues for judging height during landing. Nets, landing officers, and later modifications reduce the danger, but carrier design still matured through accidents and hard-earned operating experience.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Hosho, Ryujo, and Soryu and argues that larger carriers carry more aircraft per ton.
The transcript criticizes flush-deck layouts because pilots can struggle to judge height above the landing deck.
The transcript discusses Langley's safety net, early landing accidents, and the consequences of striking the deck too low.

segments.summary: Comparisons with Ryujo and Soryu show why larger carriers become more aircraft-efficient, while Hosho's flush-deck experience exposes the danger of judging landing height without an island reference.

segments.title: Hōshō links carrier aviation to engines and industrial transfer
segments.body: Hōshō's Mitsubishi B1M torpedo bomber illustrates how early strike aircraft were designed around a large engine and the ability to carry a torpedo. Its long service reflects reliability at a time when aircraft improvement depended heavily on gradual gains in engine power and power density. The carrier initially used imported Gloster Sparrowhawk fighters before Mitsubishi fielded the 1MF. British designer Herbert Smith, Jack Hyland, and six other engineers moved from the closed Sopwith firm to help Mitsubishi establish its fighter-design capability. The air group therefore reveals that learning to operate a carrier and learning to manufacture suitable aircraft were parts of the same industrial programme.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces the Mitsubishi B1M, emphasizes its reliability, and connects aircraft development to incremental engine improvement.
The transcript identifies the imported Gloster Sparrowhawk and the British design team that helped Mitsubishi establish fighter development.

segments.summary: Hōshō's early air group shows Japan combining dependable torpedo aircraft, imported fighters, and British engineering expertise to build a domestic aviation industry.

segments.title: Early arresting wires leave deck crews catching aircraft by hand
segments.body: The Mitsubishi 1MF used claw-type gear with longitudinal British-style arresting wires. These wires were intended mainly to stop an aircraft veering over the deck edge rather than to provide a modern arrested landing. At the low speeds of the period, deck crews could still be expected to stop a moving aircraft with their hands. Gloves arrived only later because navies initially worried that they might damage the aircraft's fabric. The practice was widespread among early carrier navies and placed considerable risk on deck crews.

evidence.note: The transcript describes claw gear and longitudinal wires intended to keep aircraft from going over the carrier's side.
The transcript says deck crews stopped aircraft by hand, explains why gloves were delayed, and notes that multiple navies shared the practice.

segments.summary: Hōshō's claw gear and longitudinal deck wires reveal how primitive carrier recovery systems shifted extraordinary risk onto sailors working beside landing aircraft.

segments.title: The Mitsubishi 1MF turns imitation into controlled industrial learning
segments.body: Comparing the Mitsubishi 1MF with the Gloster Sparrowhawk shows a controlled transition into domestic fighter design. The Japanese aircraft is only slightly faster and has somewhat less endurance, but its more powerful engine gives it a substantially higher service ceiling. Despite different weights and horsepower, the two fighters retain roughly the same power-to-weight relationship. That continuity reduces the risk of producing an unusable first design while Mitsubishi develops its own infrastructure and knowledge. The 1MF provides a viable foundation for a new carrier-fighter industry without attempting a revolutionary leap.

evidence.note: The transcript compares the Sparrowhawk and 1MF in speed, endurance, ceiling, and climb performance.
The transcript compares engine power and power-to-weight ratios and describes the 1MF as a viable development point for Japanese industry.

segments.summary: Comparing the 1MF with the Sparrowhawk shows Japan preserving familiar handling while using more engine power and a higher ceiling to establish domestic fighter production.

segments.title: Japan sees carriers as an industrial offset
segments.body: In this interpretation, Japan's geography and comparatively limited heavy industrial base make carriers more attractive than battleships. A battleship locks a navy into armour, turrets, shells, and expensive heavy manufacturing, while a carrier can change combat power by changing aircraft and aircraft weapons. Even converting a heavy naval shell into an aircraft bomb is less demanding than rebuilding a ship around a new gun system. Carriers remain expensive and complex, but they offer a more adaptable route to striking power under industrial pressure.

evidence.note: The transcript says Japan is trying to square its geography, empire, and relatively smaller peer-power industrial capacity.
The transcript says an aircraft carrier is industrially less complicated than a battleship because it avoids turrets and massive armor plate.
The transcript says aircraft and aircraft weapons can be changed more easily than battleship guns and shells.
The transcript says Hosho and Langley are both developing strike carriers while Japan and the United States justify aircraft carriers as fighting assets.

segments.summary: Aircraft carriers offered Japan a way to punch above its industrial weight among peer naval powers.

segments.title: Mahan and Corbett frame different carrier arguments
segments.body: Mahan should not be reduced to battles alone, nor Corbett to their opposite. Mahan explains why a political system should create a battle fleet, while Corbett explains what an established fleet enables a state to do. Langley and Hosho lean toward the first argument because the US and Japanese navies must prove that carriers are fighting assets. Hermes fits the second more closely: she supports presence, reconnaissance, commerce protection, deterrence, and aviation operations across a global maritime system.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes Mahan's justification for creating a battle fleet from Corbett's emphasis on the fleet's uses.
The transcript applies the contrast to American and Japanese strike carriers and to Hermes as a presence-oriented global aviation base.

segments.summary: Mahan and Corbett distinguish carriers justified through battle-fleet striking power from carriers justified through the wider uses of sea power.

segments.title: Hermes is a presence and information carrier
segments.body: Hermes has a different purpose from the American and Japanese strike-focused examples. Her priorities include seaplane handling, distant deployments, trade protection, reconnaissance, deterrence, and cruiser support rather than a single decisive fleet battle. A large crane and seaplane-maintenance facilities make her a mobile aviation base, while an early voyage through Hawaii to the China Station demonstrates the reach expected of her. With Flycatchers and Fairey IIIDs, her air group is built around learning what is happening and showing presence across a wide imperial maritime system.

evidence.note: The transcript says Hermes is a Corbettian construct about presence and operating around the world as a global aviation base.
The transcript lists commerce warfare, reconnaissance, conflict management, deterrence, peace-time presence, and operational experience.
The transcript discusses Hermes operating far from the UK and the difficulty of selling distant-water trade-protection carriers.
The transcript compares the air groups of Hermes, Hosho, and Langley and says Hermes is a reconnaissance and anti-reconnaissance asset.
The transcript says the Fairey III forms the core of Hermes's air group and shows a purpose centered on information and presence.

segments.summary: Hermes appears as a Royal Navy answer to global presence, reconnaissance, trade protection, and distant-water aviation support.

segments.title: Fleet Air Arm institutions shape Hermes's small air group
segments.body: The comparison of roughly thirty-six aircraft in Langley, fifteen in Hōshō, and twenty in Hermes shows that capacity reflected doctrine as well as hull size. Langley's usual split of eighteen torpedo bombers and eighteen fighters supports both a combat air patrol and a strike force. Hermes operates within a more complicated institution: the Fleet Air Arm sits inside the Royal Air Force and under Air Ministry administration even though the Admiralty pays for it and exercises operational control. The Air Ministry's downgrading of naval squadrons to smaller flights means a twenty-aircraft carrier amounts to about three six-aircraft flights with only a small margin. Fairey Flycatchers provide air defence and oppose enemy scouting, while the ship's main emphasis remains reconnaissance and presence.

evidence.note: The transcript compares the three carriers' air groups and describes Langley's torpedo-bomber and fighter split.
The transcript explains the Fleet Air Arm's place under the RAF and Air Ministry and the use of flights rather than squadrons.
The transcript assigns the Flycatcher air-defence and anti-scouting work while defining Hermes as a reconnaissance and presence asset.

segments.summary: Comparing carrier air groups reveals how Air Ministry control, flight-sized units, and reconnaissance priorities shaped the twenty aircraft carried by Hermes.

segments.title: The Fairey IIID makes Hermes an information carrier
segments.body: The Fairey IIID forms the core and majority of Hermes's air group, making reconnaissance the ship's central aviation task. It belongs to the long-lived Fairey III family, which first flew in 1917 and served across British and Commonwealth aviation. Its production run of 964 aircraft far exceeds the totals for the Douglas DT, Vought VE-7, Mitsubishi 1MF, and Mitsubishi B1M. Those numbers show how widely the Fairey design could be used and sustained over successive versions. On Hermes, that endurance supports the work of finding a threat, tracking it, and guiding the wider fleet's response.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces the Fairey IIID, describes the Fairey III family's service, and defines the aircraft as reconnaissance equipment.
The transcript compares production totals and identifies the Fairey III as the most prolific of the aircraft discussed.
The transcript says the Fairey III's place at the core of Hermes's air group demonstrates a purpose centered on information and presence.

segments.summary: The prolific Fairey IIID gives Hermes a durable reconnaissance core built to find, track, and report threats across distant stations.

segments.title: Undersea cables turn trade chokepoints into data chokepoints
segments.body: The world's undersea cable network closely overlaps its maritime trade routes. Important sea passages can therefore be data chokepoints as well as shipping chokepoints. The internet may feel intangible, but much of its international traffic depends on physical cables laid across the seabed. Damage or deliberate cutting at concentrated routes can disrupt communications as well as commerce. The comparison connects carrier-era trade protection to the continuing strategic importance of maritime infrastructure.

evidence.note: The transcript overlays undersea cables and trade routes, identifies combined data and trade chokepoints, and stresses the physical character of internet infrastructure.

segments.summary: A cable map shows that the same maritime geography can concentrate merchant traffic and the physical infrastructure of global communications.

segments.title: Trade maps explain why Britain wants different carriers
segments.body: Maritime trade routes explain why the Royal Navy's carrier needs differ from those of Japan and the United States. Britain has to consider home waters, the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean, the Far East, and exposed trade routes at the same time. Japan and the United States concentrate more heavily on the Pacific, which lets them prioritise battle-fleet carrier roles that would leave British presence and patrol missions uncovered. The comparison distinguishes a navy built for concentrated battle from one that must maintain both a battle fleet and a dispersed maritime-policing force.

evidence.note: The transcript says Royal Navy trade maps show global merchant routes and that Hermes and Argus matter for exposed routes.
The transcript contrasts British global commitments with American and Japanese strategic analysis.
The transcript says Japan focuses on Russia, America, and its area of the Pacific, with limited Indian Ocean follow-through.
The transcript says the United States is focused on the Pacific and challenges the idea that an Anglo-American naval race would automatically cause war.
The transcript says Britain needs both battle fleet and patrol fleet roles, and treaty cumulative limits hamper imperial trade protection.

segments.summary: A strategic map comparison shows Britain protecting global trade while Japan and the United States focus carrier thinking on the Pacific.

segments.title: South American dreadnoughts shape the US strategic horizon
segments.body: The global trade-map comparison gives the United States a different set of obligations from Britain, but its strategic neighbourhood is far from empty. The navies of Brazil, Argentina, and Chile had recently passed through their own dreadnought race and retained serious ships. Within living memory, those fleets could compare favourably with or exceed the US Navy at particular moments. Later American interest in acquiring a Chilean dreadnought after Pearl Harbor shows that these ships were more than curiosities. Naval power has to be measured against regional balances and wartime shortages rather than a simple permanent hierarchy.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts American commitments with Britain's and recalls the capabilities produced by the South American dreadnought race.
The transcript cites American interest in a Chilean dreadnought after Pearl Harbor as evidence of the ships' continuing value.

segments.summary: The fleets of Brazil, Argentina, and Chile remind viewers that American naval planning also faced a changing regional balance beyond the Pacific rivalry with Japan.

segments.title: Japan's Pacific threat narrative limits Indian Ocean strategy
segments.body: Japan's strategic narrative responds to two historic pressures: repeated conflict with Russia in Asia and the American forced opening associated with Commodore Perry. The history contains more nuance, but this was the threat framework shaping naval discussion. The resulting concept focuses on dominating Japan's part of the Pacific rather than sustaining a global maritime system. In 1942 the Indian Ocean raid damages British forces and pushes the Eastern Fleet onto the defensive, making the operation a strategic success in that limited sense. Japan has no developed plan to exploit its access to the Indian Ocean because its operational thinking had not extended that far.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the Japanese strategic narrative around Russia, Commodore Perry, and Pacific dominance while noting historical nuance.
The transcript treats the 1942 Indian Ocean operation as a limited success but says Japan lacked a developed plan for exploiting the theatre.

segments.summary: Japan's memory of Russia and Commodore Perry concentrates planning on the Pacific, helping explain why the 1942 Indian Ocean raid had little operational follow-through.

segments.title: Naval races contribute to war scares but do not cause wars alone
segments.body: A postwar Anglo-American naval race would not by itself have produced war. Qualitative competition over better ships and guns had occurred repeatedly without conflict, including British rivalry with France in the nineteenth century. Quantitative competition is more dangerous because governments begin counting whether they have enough ships to deter or defeat one another. That arithmetic adds fear, encourages alliance formation, and creates conditions in which an unrelated crisis can escalate. War still requires political causes, decisions, and miscalculations. A naval race is a symptom and contributor to a dangerous international system rather than a sufficient cause on its own.

evidence.note: The transcript rejects an automatic Anglo-American war and begins distinguishing qualitative from quantitative naval competition.
The transcript uses gun and fleet examples to explain why quantitative races add fear and alliances.
The transcript calls naval races a symptom and contributor rather than a direct cause of war.

segments.summary: Qualitative competition differs from quantitative fleet races, and naval rivalry can encourage fear and alliances without automatically causing war.

segments.title: A maritime police role requires both battle and patrol fleets
segments.body: A navy without global policing duties can concentrate more heavily on a battle fleet. A state responsible for maritime security across trade routes needs that concentrated force and a dispersed patrol fleet at the same time. Britain faces a problem similar to France being grouped with Italy despite their different commitments and geography. Carrier and cruiser tonnage limits therefore bite harder against navies whose ships must cover imperial and commercial routes. Britain's preference for more 6-inch cruisers over fewer 8-inch cruisers reflects the search for hull numbers, yet the fleet still lacks enough units for every duty.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes a concentrated battle fleet from the additional patrol fleet required by a maritime-policing role.
The transcript compares French and British treaty problems arising from different commitments and geography.
The transcript connects British 6-inch cruiser preferences and carrier limits to the shortage of hulls for trade protection.

segments.summary: Global maritime security demands dispersed patrol forces as well as a concentrated battle fleet, making treaty equality especially restrictive for Britain and France.

segments.title: Treaty tonnage limits close off a Hermes-style fleet
segments.body: The closing argument connects cruiser definitions, carrier tonnage, and the Royal Navy's missed chance to build more Hermes-like aviation presence ships. If the treaty threshold had been higher, Hermes, Langley, and Hosho might not have counted as carrier tonnage at all. Britain could then have paired one small aviation ship with every five or six cruisers, creating a distinct light-carrier structure for distant stations. The treaty system instead forces the Royal Navy to choose between fleet carriers and the dispersed presence missions Hermes was designed to cover.

evidence.note: The transcript says a higher cruiser threshold could have left Hermes, Langley, and Hosho outside carrier tonnage limits.
The transcript argues Britain might have built more Hermes-like ships and created a light-carrier structure.
The transcript says cumulative limits prevent Britain from using Hermes-style carriers for South Atlantic, East China Sea, and Indian Ocean presence.

segments.summary: A treaty counterfactual asks how carrier development changes if small carriers do not count against cumulative carrier tonnage.

segments.title: Hōshō, Langley, and Hermes embody three national strategies
segments.body: The three ships are unusually clear products of national strategy before treaty rules further distorted their development. Hōshō gives Japan an edge that may offset limits in heavy industry. Langley gives the United States practical knowledge about how carriers and their air groups can be employed. Hermes gives Britain presence and security across trade routes that cannot all be covered by the battle fleet. Her completion is tied to peacetime deterrence and avoiding a repetition of World War I disruption by surface raiders and submarines rather than matching a later fleet carrier's strike capacity.

evidence.note: The transcript summarizes the three national aims as Japanese advantage, American employment knowledge, and British presence and security.
The transcript connects Hermes's completion to peacetime security and protection against surface-raider and subsurface threats.

segments.summary: The conclusion reduces the comparison to three aims: a Japanese combat edge, American operational knowledge, and British presence and trade security.

segments.title: A larger Hawkins design reshapes the carrier treaty counterfactual
segments.body: The closing question begins with British cruiser design choices during the First World War. An alternative Hawkins concept displaced roughly 15,000 tons and carried four triple 9.2-inch turrets, unlike the smaller 7.5-inch-gunned compromise that entered service. The compromise emerged from speed, gun-supply, and stopping-power calculations as well as Winston Churchill's preference for smaller, faster ships over proposals supported by Admiral Battenberg. If the larger cruiser had defined the treaty threshold, carriers below 15,000 tons might have escaped the category limits that constrained Hermes-like vessels. Germany would still face the separate 10,000-ton restriction of the Treaty of Versailles, potentially forcing a different answer to foreign 12-gun cruisers than the Deutschland class. Britain and France could build mobile aviation bases for imperial patrol and trade protection, while Japan, Italy, and the United States decided whether to answer with their own small carriers or squeeze fleet-carrier ambitions beneath the threshold. Ranger's standard displacement just below 15,000 tons makes the hypothetical especially revealing because a different legal category might have changed what the US Navy asked the ship to do.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the larger Hawkins design discussion, including roughly 15,000 tons and four triple 9.2-inch turrets, and explains the smaller compromise adopted.
The transcript asks how a 15,000-ton threshold might change small-carrier building by Britain, France, Italy, Japan, and the United States.
The transcript uses Ranger's sub-15,000-ton standard displacement to ask whether she would remain a fleet carrier or answer a new presence-carrier category.

segments.summary: The final counterfactual traces how a 15,000-ton, 9.2-inch-gunned Hawkins concept might have raised treaty thresholds and encouraged a separate family of small presence carriers.
